title: Atomic structure and the periodic table flash cards

cards.front: Define an element.
back: A substance containing atoms with the same number of protons.

cards.front: What is the atomic number of an atom?
back: Its number of protons.

cards.front: Name the particle with no charge and relative mass 1.
back: Neutron.

cards.front: Which separation method recovers an insoluble solid from a liquid?
back: Filtration.

cards.front: Give the electron arrangement of calcium, atomic number 20.
How does boiling point change down Group 0?
back: It increases.

cards.front: Explain the difference between a compound and a mixture.
back: In a compound, different elements are **chemically combined in fixed proportions**.
In a mixture, substances are **not chemically combined** and can be separated by physical methods.

cards.front: Explain why a neutral atom has no overall charge.
back: It has **equal numbers of protons and electrons**.
Their equal but opposite charges **cancel**.

cards.front: Explain why chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are isotopes of the same element.
back: They have the **same number of protons**.
They have **different numbers of neutrons**.

cards.front: A sodium atom loses one electron. Explain why the resulting ion is positive and why it is still sodium.
back: It now has one more positive proton than negative electrons, giving a **+1 charge**.
The number of **protons is unchanged**, so its identity is unchanged.

cards.front: Explain why helium is unreactive even though it has only two electrons.
back: Its first electron shell is **full**.
This is a **stable arrangement**, so it does not readily gain, lose or share electrons.

cards.front: Why did Mendeleev sometimes place elements out of strict atomic-weight order?
back: He wanted elements with **similar chemical properties in the same group**.
Strict atomic-weight order sometimes put elements in **inappropriate groups**.

cards.front: Give two physical differences between a typical transition metal and a Group 1 metal.
back: A transition metal generally has a **higher melting point**.
It generally has a **higher density**.

cards.front: Describe two features of the plum pudding model.
back: A **ball of positive charge**.
**Negative electrons embedded** within it; no central nucleus.

cards.front: An aluminium-27 ion has atomic number 13 and charge 3+. Calculate its numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons.
back: Protons = **13**.
Electrons = 13 − 3 = **10**.

cards.front: An element contains 60% isotope of mass 10 and 40% isotope of mass 11. Calculate its relative atomic mass.
back: Divide by the total percentage: 1,040 ÷ 100.
**Aᵣ = 10.4**, with no unit.

cards.front: Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium.
back: Its outer electron is **farther from the nucleus**, with more occupied shells.
Increased **shielding and distance reduce the attraction** to the outer electron.
The electron is **lost more easily**, so potassium reacts more readily.

cards.front: Explain why chlorine is more reactive than bromine.
back: Chlorine has **fewer occupied electron shells**.
There is less distance/shielding, giving a **stronger nuclear attraction for an incoming electron**.
Chlorine gains an electron more readily.

cards.front: Write a balanced equation for sodium reacting with water and state what makes the final solution alkaline.
back: **2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂**.
The product **sodium hydroxide** supplies hydroxide ions in solution, making it alkaline.

cards.front: Explain how later discoveries supported Mendeleev’s periodic table.
back: He left **gaps** for undiscovered elements.
He **predicted their properties** from surrounding elements.
Newly discovered elements had properties that **matched the predictions**, supporting the table.

cards.front: A typical atom has radius 0.10 nm. Convert this to metres and compare it with a nucleus of radius 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ m.
back: The atom’s radius is **10,000 times** the nuclear radius.

cards.front: Chlorine is added to potassium bromide solution. Write the balanced full and ionic equations and explain why the reaction occurs.
back: Full: **Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂**.
Ionic: **Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂**.
Chlorine is **more reactive than bromine**, so it displaces bromine from bromide.
Potassium ions are **spectator ions** and do not change.

cards.front: Explain four choices made when separating ink by paper chromatography.
back: Use **pencil** for the baseline because it does not dissolve and separate like ink.
Keep the baseline **above the solvent level** so the sample is not washed into the solvent.
Use small spots so components begin in a narrow region and can separate clearly.
Mark the **solvent front promptly** before evaporation makes its position unclear.

cards.front: Compare simple and fractional distillation and give an example of each.
back: Both **evaporate a liquid and condense its vapour** for collection.
Simple distillation recovers a solvent, such as **water from salt solution**.
Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids, such as **ethanol and water**, using their different boiling points.
A fractionating column provides **repeated evaporation and condensation**, improving separation.

cards.front: How many oxygen and hydrogen atoms are represented in Ca(OH)₂?
back: Two oxygen atoms and two hydrogen atoms, because the subscript multiplies the complete OH group.

cards.front: What does the coefficient 2 in 2MgO multiply?
back: The whole formula, giving two Mg atoms and two O atoms in total.

cards.front: Why does changing a subscript not simply balance an equation?
back: It changes the composition and identity of the substance. Balance using coefficients instead.

cards.front: Why do isotopes of an element have very similar chemical reactions?
back: Their neutral atoms have the same electron arrangement, including the same outer electrons.

cards.front: What denominator is used for a weighted mean from isotope counts?
back: The total number counted. Divide by 100 only when using percentage abundances.

cards.front: What is a useful check on an isotope weighted mean?
back: It should lie between the isotope masses and be closer to the more abundant isotope.

cards.front: Why did leaving gaps strengthen Mendeleev’s table?
back: It kept similar elements grouped and generated predictions that later discoveries could test.

cards.front: Why does a modern periodic-table box not identify just one isotope?
back: It represents the element defined by proton number; its relative atomic mass averages naturally occurring isotope abundances.

cards.front: How would you recover both sand and solid salt from salty water containing sand?
back: Filter to recover sand, then concentrate and cool the filtrate to crystallise salt.

cards.front: Which method would recover water rather than salt from the filtrate?
back: Simple distillation: evaporate the water and collect it after condensation.

cards.front: Can evaporation occur below the boiling point?
back: Yes. It occurs at the surface, whereas boiling occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling temperature.

cards.front: Why is a white chloride formed by reacting an alkali metal with chlorine not necessarily a precipitate?
back: A precipitate is an insoluble solid formed from solution. Direct combination can form a white solid without precipitation.

cards.front: Why do Group 1 and Group 7 show opposite reactivity trends?
back: Larger, more shielded atoms lose an outer electron more easily in Group 1, but attract an incoming electron less strongly in Group 7.

cards.front: Are noble gases normally diatomic molecules?
back: No. They exist as individual atoms with stable full outer electron shells.
